extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, economists, students of political economy, and the informed public interested in taxation policy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for evaluating methods of raising public revenue (tax policy), with an argument that a tax on land values best satisfies these principles. Focuses on effects on prices, production, equality, certainty, administrative feasibility, and social outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheapness / Economy of collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus in all respects a tax upon land values is the cheapest tax by which a large revenue can be raised—giving to the government the largest net revenue in proportion to the amount taken from the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes that add to prices are shifted along the chain (manufacturer → jobber → retailer → consumer) and increase as they go, so consumers pay much more than the government receives. Example: Manila cigars bought in San Francisco costing $70 a thousand, of which $56 is customs duty; each dealer charges profit on the full taxed amount. Because land is not produced by human labor, a tax on rent does not check supply and therefore does not create the same cascading burdens; a land-value tax yields largest net revenue relative to burden on people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainty is an important element in taxation ... will opportunities for tyranny and corruption be opened on the one side, and for evasions and frauds on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncertain taxes (e.g., whisky and tobacco, customs undervaluations, untruthful income returns) cause corruption, evasion, and large material loss (costs of enforcement, bribes, smugglers' expenses). A tax on land values possesses the element of certainty because land is immovable and unconcealable; it can be assessed and collected with definiteness and 'to the last cent.' Were taxes placed upon land values irrespective of improvements, the scheme would be simple and valuations would be made with comparable certainty to a real-estate agent's pricing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality (ability-to-pay / proportionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam Smith's canon is, that 'The subjects of every state ought to contribute toward the support of the government as nearly as possible in proportion to their respective abilities ...' The tax upon land values is, therefore, the most just and equal of all taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect taxes fall unequally (e.g., families with many dependents pay more on consumables). Direct equal charges per individual are also unjust because incomes support differing numbers of persons. Land-value taxation is justified because land rent represents value created by the community (grows with population) and falls on those who receive peculiar community-created benefit; taxing that rent in proportion to benefit achieves equality of contribution without penalizing productive labor or capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-shifting / stable incidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax on rent would fall wholly on landlords, and could not be shifted to any class of consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes on manufactures or imported goods are shifted through prices; land-value tax cannot be shifted because it does not increase the cost of production or reduce supply. The immobility and fixed supply of land prevent shifting of the tax burden to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-distortion / Economic efficiency (do not discourage production)
rubrics_metrics.description: The way taxes raise prices is by increasing the cost of production, and checking supply. But land is not a thing of human production, and taxes upon rent cannot check supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes on production, improvements, machinery, or stock act like fines on industry and discourage planting, building, drainage, manufacturing, and investment—thus reducing production. Substituting a land-value tax for such taxes would remove these disincentives, stimulate production, and allow labor and capital to receive full rewards, increasing the common wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity / Administrative clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Were all taxes placed upon land values, irrespective of improvements, the scheme of taxation would be so simple and clear, and public attention would be so directed to it, that the valuation of taxation could and would be made with the same certainty that a real estate agent can determine the price a seller can get for a lot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single tax on land values would simplify revenue collection, reduce opportunities for bribery and evasion, and make the tax system more transparent to the public, thereby improving compliance and reducing administrative cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessability / separability of land value and improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The only objection ... is that from the difficulty of separation, we might, in taxing the rent of land, tax something else. But, as a matter of fact, the value of land can always be readily distinguished from the value of improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where land has never been improved, or where buildings and land are separately owned, or where fire destroys improvements leaving land value, assessors can separate land and improvement values. Practical separation of clearly distinguishable recent improvements suffices for justice and policy; absolute accuracy is impossible but unnecessary. Long-ago permanent works may be treated as part of land value as generations pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political economy / interest-group resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The tax on land values is the only tax of any importance that does not distribute itself. Hence, a large and powerful class are directly interested in keeping down the tax on land values ... There is, thus, a definite and powerful interest opposed to the taxation of land values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other taxes have organized beneficiaries who do not oppose them; protective tariffs and excises have been sustained by special interests. Political feasibility must account for the fact that landowners will resist a land-value tax, while many consumers and producers are unaware of or indifferent to indirect taxes. Popular understanding could, however, create a political coalition to implement the reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on land use and allocation (anti-speculation / promote improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax on land values tends to increase the competition between owners, and thus to reduce the price of land ... No one would care to hold land unless to use it, and land now withheld from use would everywhere be thrown open to improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A land-value tax would lower selling prices, end land speculation, open vast tracts to settlers and cultivation, force urban vacant lots and mineral lands into productive use, and eliminate the bonus required to obtain land. It would operate to force improvement rather than penalize it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional and labor-market effects
rubrics_metrics.description: To shift the burden of taxation from production and exchange to the value or rent of land would ... make employers compete for laborers, and wages would rise to the fair earnings of labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting land-value taxation for taxes on production would equalize wealth distribution, raise the poorest above abject poverty, cut down overgrown fortunes, increase the number of conscious landholders, and lead to higher wages as employers compete for labor rather than labor undercutting wages in competition for jobs.
